lawyer:
M. Fazlul Karim With Nurul Islam Chowdhury ----- For the Appellant. 
Sharifuddin Chaklader ----- For the Respondent
parties:
Abdur Razzak ----- Appellant
Vs.
Rabeya Khatun ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is against the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge, reversing those passed by the learned Munsif, Second Court, Chittagong, in a suit for partition.

2. The plaintiffs case in short is that the land in suit previously belonged to one Wahed Ali who executed a deed of gift in the year 1925 A.D. in favour of his sisters sons Thanda Mia and Omra Mia defendant Nos. 2 and 5 respectively and delivery of possession of the same to them. The defendants Nos. 1 and 5 since the gift continued to remain in possession of the suit land and the said property was recorded in C.S. record of right in the name of both the defendants in 4 annas share each of the entire land being the gifted property. The remaining 8 annas share of the property was recorded in the names of his 2 daughters namely Ambia defendant No. 3), Rabya Khatun (defendant No. 1) and his wife. When defendant Nos. 1 and 5 had been in possession of the gifted property the plaintiff purchased the 4 annas of defendant No. 5, Orma Mia by a registered sale deed in the year 959 A.D. vide Ext. 1 and his name had been recorded in the S.A. khatian to the extent of his purchase. But as there was difficulty in possessing ejmali he demanded partition, but being refused he brought the suit for partition and for separate saham of his purchased share.

3. Rabya Khatun, the daughter of Wahed Ali, being defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement, denying all the material allegations made in the plaint, contending, inter al in that the deed of gift executed in 1925 A.D. by her father in favour of the defendant No. 2 and 5 was not a gift but a will which was subsequently cancelled by her father by another deed of cancellation in the year 1930 A.D. and therefore she along with her other sister Ambia Khatun and her mother became the sole heirs of Wahed Ali after his death and the defendants 1 and 5 having lost all interest in any portion of the suit land the plaintiff acquired no interest by his purchase from Omra Mia in 1959 A.D. vide Ext. 1 and he being not a co-sharer no question of partition could arise.

4. On these pleadings the parties fought out the suit. The court of first instance on a consideration of the pleading of the parties and the evidence on record came to the view that the disputed document namely, Ext. A (1) was not a Will but a Gift which could not be cancelled subsequently after the gift took its effect and the said deed of gift having all legal force the plaintiff was entitled on purchase from Omra Mia, 4 annas share and on a further finding that the gift in the favour of defendant Nos. 1 and 5 having been followed by delivery of possession, the condition attached to the deed of gift as to the provisions of reserving life usufruct of the said property with the donor would be void and in that view of the matter the suit was decreed directing separate saham of the plaintiff on partition. On appeal the said was revered by the Subordinate Judge, on a finding that the said gift having reserved the usufruct and control of the said property with the donor it was a gift to take effect. In future and as it was not accompanied by delivery of possession the said would not operate until the death of Wahed Ali. In that view of the matter the court of appeal below came to a finding that the gift was absolutely void. The court on further finding that the plaintiff's possession, if any, was not on the strength of the gift allowed the appeal with cost. The judgment and decree of the court of first instance were set aside and plaintiff's suit was dismissed with costs. As against that the plaintiffs have preferred this appeal to this court.

5. Mr. Nurul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal having taken me through the judgments of both the courts below and evidence on record, has urged that the court of appeal below erred in law in holding that the condition as mentioned in the deed of gift reserving usufruct to the donor of life would invalidate the gift. He has further urged that the court of appeal below on a misconstruction and misreading of the deed of gift came to an erroneous finding that it provided no scope for any possession for the plaintiff and upon a non-consideration of such evidence on record as to plaintiff's possession came to an erroneous finding that the plaintiff was not in possession on the strength of the deed of gift. The said finding having been arrived at upon a misconstruction of the title deed of the plaintiff and upon non-consideration of the material evidence on record, needs to be set aside.

6. Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1, has, on the other hand, urged that a gift by a Muslim is never valid if not accompanied by delivery of possession and, in support of this contention he has referred to the decision reported in 98 I.C. at page 285, A.I.R. 1926 Born at page 559 and I.L.R. Cal. at page 138.

7. In this appeal the point of law that arises from determination is simple. This is whether a gift reserving usufruct in favour of the donor for life would be a void. There is no dispute to the proposition of law that a gift by a Mohammaden, whether registered or unregistered, would not take affect as a valid gift unless accompanied by delivery of possession and that a gift which purports to postpone possession to a future date would be void. The decisions relied upon by Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, reiterated, that principle of law with which I am in respectful agreement.

<u>8. In the case of a transfer by way of gift it is the duty of a court to look into the deed itself in order to find out the scope of the same and the intention of the donor as spelt out in the deed itself because the essential conditions of a valid gift are that the donor must have intended a gift and an immediate gift intending to transfer the ownership of the property without consideration voluntarily and accepted by the donee being accompanied by delivery of possession of the corpus. For that purpose one has to look at the instrument creating the gift and construe the same as one finds it without changing or altering the terms of the deed by outside evidence. On a reference to the deed or gift as evidence by Ext. A (1) it is seen that the recital of the said deed in the relevant portion runs thus:"</u>

<u>"You being my daughters sons I have a great love for both of you and having satisfied with the care you have taken of me during my illness I hereby make this gift to you of the property in schedule but the said property would be kept for my maintenance till my death and after my death you will have all the right in the land gifted to you."</u>

<u>From a clear reading of the said it would be evident that by the said recital in the deed the donor only reserved a life interest as to the usufruct. The said reservation of the usufruct is not prohibited under the principle of Mohammadan law as under the Mohammadan law the corpus may be vested in one person and the usufruct vested on another person. Under the principle of Mohammadan law: When a gift is made with a condition which derogates from the completeness of the grant the condition would be void and the gift will take effect as if no conditions were attached with. Thus, a gift restraining delivery of immediate possession of the corpus would be derogatory to the completeness of the grant and the said condition would be void but reserving usufruct for the life with the donor would not be a condition derogatory to the completeness of the grant, as under the Mohammadan law as stated herein before, the corpus may rest in one person and the usufruct on another person. Under the Mohammadan law a life interest thus, can be created by means of a gift in favour of the donee in the gifted property and in same way the usufruct of the gifted property could also be kept with the donor for life and in the latter the gift will take effect subject to the condition of reserving the usufruct with the donee for life as in that case the usufruct will vest in one person and the corpus in another person. If the donor transfers a property to the donee by a deed of gift without reserving any domination over the corpus, merely the existence of a condition that the whole or a part of the usufruct would be paid to the donor or would be kept for his use during his life the said would not invalidate the transfer by gift. Similarly, if a Muslim makes a gift to one person of certain property on condition that the income of the property or a part of the income of the property gifted shall not belong to the donee but shall he used for the benefit of another person during his life time, the said gift shall also be valid.</u>

9. In the view I have taken herein before I am supported by a number of decisions and of good authorities. Sir John Wedge in delivering the judgment of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Mohammad Abdul Ghani Vs. Fakher Jahan Begum and others, reported in 49. Indian Appeals, at page 195 in the relevant portion of the judgment observed thus:

"The reserving of the usufruct did not by itself make the gift of the property now in question void under Muslim law .....For a valid gift under Mohammadan law three conditions are necessary, which their Lordships consider have been correctly stated thus;- (a) manifestation of the wish to give on the part of the donor; (b) the acceptance of the donee, either impliedly or expressly; and (c) the taking of possession of the subject matter Of the gift by the donee, either actually or constructively. The question is did Lutf Ullah Khan actually or constructively take possession of the property in question in this suit. That he did not, until Munni Bibi's death in 1906, take physical possession of Mouza Mundia Misir, the 4 annas 5 pies share in Gundia or the two groves, house and sir land in Jalalpur, or apply for mutation of names in his favour in respect of these particular properties, is admitted. On the execution of the deed of gift in 1884, Lutfullah Khan did obtain mutation of names in his favour of all the other Zamindari property, and from March, 7, 1884 until Munni Bibi died in 1906 he paid the Government revenue which became due in respect of the talukdari part of the property now in question. If Lutfullah Khan had received after March 7, 1884, and before Munni Bibi died in 1906, any of the rents or profits of the property now in question he would be held to have received them as a trustee for Munni although the title to the corpus of the property was in him. In their Lordships opinion Lutfullah Khan must be regarded as having been constructively in possession although not in physical possession of the corpus of the property now in question from 1884 until 1906, and the gift was valid gift".

<u>10. I am in respectful agreement with the observations as above to the effect that reservation of usufruct by the deed itself would not invalidate a gift made by a Mohammadan under the Mohammadan law and that the possession of a donee could be affected either by actual possession or by constructive possession which constructive possession could be evidenced by the mutation of the records of right in the name of the donee are in complete accord with the view I have taken herein before.</u>

11. In support of this principle reference may also be made to the decision of the Privy Council in the case of Newarish Ali Khan Vs. Ali Reza khan. In that case a similar point was involved and their Lordships of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council held in the relevant portion of the judgment as under:- "What Muslim law does recognise and insist upon is. the distinction between the corpus of the property itself and the usufruct in the property. Over the corpus of the property the law recognises only absolute dominion heritable, and unrestricted in point of time and where a gift of the corpus seeks to impose condition inconsistent with such absolute dominion, the condition is rejected as repugnant but interest limited in point of time can be created in usufruct of the property and the dominion over the corpus takes effect subject to any such limited interest."

12. The principle thus enunciated was followed in the case of Mst. Khan Bibi Vs. Mst. Sufia Begum, reported in P.L.D. 1969 Lah. at page 388, Lad Jan Vs. Mohammad Shaft Allan, reported in I.L.R. 34 All at page 478. Following those authorities as quoted above I find that the finding of the court of appeal below to the effect that the said condition reserving the usufruct for the life time of the donee and control over said usufruct would make the gift a contingent gift purported to take effect in future and thus a void gift is wholly erroneous as in the said document (Ext. A (1) there is nothing to how that the possession or dominion over the corpus of the said property was also reserved or postponed to a future date. That the said was not the intention would be evident by the entry in the records of right of the entire gifted property of the donor in the name of the donee namely, Thanda Mia and Omra Mia in the R.S. Records. The said R.S. khatian was prepared in the year 1929 and completed in 1930 immediately after the deed of gift was executed and registered in 1925 without any objection from the donor. An entry in the khatian is not an evidence of title by itself but it is an evidence of possession and a strong presumptive evidence of title also (Ref: 30 D.L.R. (S.C.) 81 and following the principle as enunciated by the Privy Council in the case referred to earlier the donee would be considered to be in constructive possession of the said gifted property and would be construed that the said gift was in fact followed by possession as evidenced by the entry in the C.S. khatian in the names of the donee. There is evidence on record that the donor died long before and the defendants donee had been in possession of the suit land since after the death of Wahed Ali.

The court of appeal below had not considered this legal aspect of this matter.

13. The court of appeal below however took notice of the fact that the name of the plaintiffs vendor was recorded in the R.S. khatian and having taking notice of the said the learned court took the view that through the said was recorded as such the said entry was absolutely void and without basis as the gift itself was void ab initio. If the deed of gift was a valid one, the said entry perhaps could have been taken into consideration by the court of appeal below, in proving prima facie the plaintiffs vendors possession of the gifted suit land, to the extent of his 4 annas share.

<u>14. The construction of a title document is a question of law. Findings of fact arrived at by misconstruction of a document are liable to be set aside in second appeal but only when the said document was a document of title and was the foundation of a suit, being in the nature of a contract or a document of title and hence the construction of a kabuliyat or the construction of an entry in a khatian used as a document of title or the construction of a deed, purporting to be a deed of gift would amount to a question of law (Refer 120 I.C. at page 557). In the instant case the court of appeal below arrived at the finding of fact to the effect that the gift was not a void gift as it purported to take effect in future by reserving the usufruct was arrived at on a misreading and misconstruction of the document of gift and upon a wrong view of the law, causing an error of law affecting the merits of the case and thus it needs to be set aside. The finding of the court of appeal below as to possession was also arrived at only on a consideration of the fact that as the gift was void there could not be any question of possession on the strength of the gift which was again erroneous as it was arrived at without taking into consideration the presumption of correctness attached to an entry in the R.S. khatian and without taking into consideration the evidence as to the possession of the plaintiff evidenced by the entry in the R.S. khatian and the evidence on record and without taking into consideration the legal position that even a possession under a document of title which subsequently proved to be a void document, would create a title in favour of the possessor if possessed for a period of more than 12 years, by adverse possession. On the premises above I find enough substance in this appeal and the said need to be allowed.</u>

In the result, this appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree of the court of appeal below are set aside and those of the trial court is restored. But in the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs before this court.

End.
